title: Origin, languages, and jobs
goal: Say your country, nationality, the languages you speak, and your job — with one magic ending that builds them all.
bekal: form nationality words and language names from country names
say which languages you speak, and how well

dialogs.title: گفتگو — در کافهٔ مؤسسهٔ زبان
dialogs.intro: A small café next to a language institute. Budi sits alone with a book open; a woman at the next table speaks to him.

lines.speaker: مریم:
lines.id: Excuse me, are you a student?

lines.speaker: بودی:
lines.text: بله، من دانشجویِ زبانِ فارسی هستم.
lines.baca: bale, man dâneshju-ye zabân-e fârsi hastam.
lines.id: Yes, I'm a student of Persian.
lines.literal: yes, I student-of language-of Persian am-I.

lines.speaker: مریم:
lines.id: How interesting! Where are you from?

lines.speaker: بودی:
lines.text: من اندونزیایی هستم، اهلِ جاکارتا. شما؟
lines.baca: man andoneziyâyi hastam, ahl-e Jâkârtâ. shomâ?
lines.id: I'm Indonesian, from Jakarta. And you?
lines.literal: I Indonesia-i am-I, native-of Jakarta. you?

lines.speaker: مریم:
lines.text: من ایرانی‌ام. اسمِ من مریم است. مترجمم.
lines.baca: man irâni-am. esm-e man Maryam ast. motarjemam.
lines.id: I'm Iranian. My name is Maryam. I'm a translator.
lines.literal: I Iran-i-I. name-of I Maryam is. translator-I.

lines.speaker: بودی:
lines.id: How many languages do you speak?

lines.speaker: مریم:
lines.text: فارسی، عربی و انگلیسی. کمی هم ترکی.
lines.baca: fârsi, arabi va engelisi. kami ham torki.
lines.id: Persian, Arabic, and English. A little Turkish too.
lines.literal: Persian, Arabic and English. a-little also Turkish.

lines.speaker: بودی:
lines.text: عالی است! من فقط اندونزیایی و کمی فارسی بلدم.
lines.baca: âli ast! man faghat andoneziyâyi va kami fârsi baladam.
lines.id: Amazing! I only speak Indonesian and a little Persian.
lines.literal: amazing is! I only Indonesia-i and a-little Persian know-I.

lines.speaker: بودی:
lines.text: لطف دارید. من هنوز مبتدی هستم.
lines.baca: lotf dârid. man hanuz mobtadi hastam.
lines.id: That's kind of you. I'm still a beginner.
lines.literal: kindness have-you. I still beginner am-I.

lines.speaker: مریم:
lines.id: Are you here as a student or an employee?

lines.speaker: بودی:
lines.text: من مهندسم. اینجا برایِ کار هستم.
lines.baca: man mohandesam. injâ barâye kâr hastam.
lines.id: I'm an engineer. I'm here for work.
lines.literal: I engineer-I. here for-of work am-I.

notes: ⚠️ **Nationality words don't change for gender.** Reza اندونزیایی, Maryam also اندونزیایی. If you've studied Arabic (اندونيسي / اندونيسية) or Russian (индонезиец / индонезийка), this is a real relief: Persian nouns carry no trace of gender at all.

**Jobs take no article.** من مهندسم = "I'm engineer", never "I'm *an* engineer". Persian has no *a* / *an* / ال here, so drop the article you'd use in English — just as French *je suis ingénieur* does.

***Che*** **+ word = an exclamation.** چه جالب! ("how interesting!"), چه خوب! ("how nice!"), چه گرم! ("how hot!"). With a noun and adjective, add the ending ـی at the end: چه روزِ خوبی! ("what a lovely day!") — that pattern returns in unit 3.

⚠️ **You will almost certainly hear** فارسیِ شما خیلی خوب است **("your Persian is very good").** Say three words of Persian in Iran and someone will praise you lavishly. Don't take it literally and don't argue at length — answer لطف دارید (*lotf dârid*, "you're very kind") or خواهش می‌کنم. This is your first taste of تعارف (*ta'arof*), the layered etiquette of compliments and refusals covered fully in unit 15.

***Ahl-e kojâyid?*** **= اهلِ کجا + ید.** The شما "to be" ending (ـید) attaches straight to کجا, and since کجا ends in a vowel, a ی is inserted: کجایید. The long form اهلِ کجا هستید؟ is just as correct and easier for beginners — use whichever feels comfortable.

**Spoken Tehran forms for this dialogue:** اهلِ کجایین؟ (*ahl-e kojâyin?*), چند زبون بلدین؟ (*chand zabun baladin?*), فارسیتون خیلی خوبه (*fârsitun kheyli khube*). Notice three changes: ـید → ـین, ân → un (زبان → زبون), and است → ـه. All three are explained in full in unit 14.

grammars.title: The ending ـی: country → nationality → language
body: The ending ـی (*-i*) is one of the most productive tools in Persian. Attach it to a country name and you get the nationality and the language name in one go — like English *Iraq → Iraqi*.
after: ⚠️ The name of the Persian language itself is **not** ایرانی but **فارسی** (*Fârsi*) — from فارس (Fars), a province in southern Iran (the Greeks' "Persis", hence "Persian"). Calling it "Iranian" isn't a big mistake, but saying فارسی instantly sounds right.

The same ending also makes adjectives from ordinary nouns: آب ("water") → آبی ("blue"), خاک ("soil, dust") → خاکی ("earth-colored" — the source of English *khaki*), جنوب ("south") → جنوبی ("southern").

Notice the pattern ـستان in country names: عربستان ("land of the Arabs"), افغانستان, تاجیکستان, هندوستان. ستان means "place, land" — a native Persian ending you'll find across a third of the map of Asia (Pakistan, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan…).

grammars.title: Asking questions without extra words
body: Persian makes questions the easy way: **the word order doesn't change at all.** No "do", no swapping "you are" to "are you" — just raise your voice at the end, as in a casual English "You're a student?"
after: For a more formal tone — in letters, interviews, the news — put آیا (*âyâ*) at the start: آیا شما ایرانی هستید؟ In everyday conversation آیا is almost never used.
Note that the Persian question mark faces the other way: **؟** — a mirror image of the Latin one, because the script runs leftward. The same goes for the comma: **،**

For questions asking for information, the question word goes **where the answer will stand** — it does not move to the front as in English: شما اهلِ **کجا** هستید؟ → من اهلِ **اندونزی** هستم. Literally "you are from *where*?" — the same order as the answer.

blocks.text: Notice the ending **ـنده** in راننده، فروشنده، نویسنده. It attaches to a verb stem and means "one who does", like English *-er*: راندن ("to drive") → راننده, فروختن ("to sell") → فروشنده, نوشتن ("to write") → نویسنده. Once you know the verb stems in unit 9, you can guess dozens of job names yourself.

blocks.title: European words that became Persian
items: Persian borrowed heavily from French in the 19th century — not from English. That's why the sounds are often surprising: مرسی (*mersi*, thanks), دوش (*dush*, shower), آسانسور (*âsânsor*, elevator), مانتو (*mânto*, coat), املت (*omlet*), بلیت (*belit*, ticket), کلاس (*kelâs*, class), دکتر (*doktor*). The traffic went both ways: English *bazaar*, *caravan*, and *pajamas* are Persian words.

If you're stuck for a modern word, try the English word with a French accent — your chances are decent. But don't overdo it: "computer" is indeed کامپیوتر and a cell phone is موبایل, but "airplane" has its own native Persian word, هواپیما (*havâpeymâ*, literally "air-measurer").

blocks.title: Three sentences to introduce yourself anywhere
items: *Salâm, esm-e man ... ast. man ahl-e Andonezi hastam.* — سلام، اسمِ من ... است. من اهلِ اندونزی هستم. ("Hello, my name is ... I'm from Indonesia.")
*Man ... hastam va injâ barâye kâr / barâye dars hastam.* — من ... هستم و اینجا برایِ کار / برایِ درس هستم. ("I'm a ... and I'm here for work / to study.")

*Fârsi-ye man hanuz khub nist, vali yâd migiram.* — فارسیِ من هنوز خوب نیست، ولی یاد می‌گیرم. ("My Persian isn't good yet, but I'm learning.") This last sentence gets a warm welcome wherever you say it.

items: I'm Indonesian.
How many languages do you speak?

She is a translator.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the right word of degree.
items: You don't know a single word of Turkish: ترکی ____ بلد نیستم.
You know a few words of Persian: ____ فارسی بلدم.
Your English is very good: انگلیسیِ من ____ خوب است.
You've just started and aren't fluent: من ____ مبتدی هستم.
You speak only Indonesian: ____ اندونزیایی بلدم.

من اندونزیایی هستم. — شما چند زبان بلدید؟ — او مترجم است. — من اینجا برایِ کار هستم. — من اصلاً ترکی بلد نیستم.
